title: Cooling a roof, cooling a city
bodyMd:
A city tested reflective roof coatings on twenty municipal buildings and found that the coated surfaces were cooler at midday than nearby untreated roofs. Officials proposed expanding the programme, arguing that the measured temperature difference would translate directly into lower electricity use across the city. An engineer supported further trials but resisted that inference. Surface temperature is only one part of a building's thermal behaviour: insulation, ventilation, occupancy and the timing of cooling demand also matter. A warehouse with no air-conditioning might show a large roof-temperature reduction and no electricity saving at all.

The engineer's objection was not that the coating had failed. The experiment had measured a real physical change, but the policy claim concerned a different outcome. She proposed comparing electricity use in matched occupied buildings before and after treatment, accounting for weather. That design would still not answer every question about a city-wide rollout, yet it would connect the intervention to the benefit used to justify it.
